nodes.name: Figs
nodes.desc: Strangler and tree figs bear fruit that many forest animals eat; GloBI records link fig fruit to woolly monkeys, pacas and brockets near Manú.

nodes.name: Milk tree
nodes.desc: A lowland forest tree whose fruit is recorded in GloBI as food for many birds and monkeys here, from macaws to woolly and howler monkeys.

nodes.name: Bromeliads
nodes.desc: Cloud-forest plants growing on trees and slopes. Their leaf hearts are a main food of the spectacled bear.

nodes.name: Laurel family trees
nodes.desc: Montane forest trees of the laurel family. Wikipedia notes laurels are among the fruit families Andean cock-of-the-rock eats.

nodes.name: Brown woolly monkey
nodes.desc: Mostly eats fruit, switching to leaves and insects when fruit is scarce. It is an effective seed disperser that keeps seeds in its gut for a long time.

nodes.name: South American tapir
nodes.desc: A big lowland forest browser and fruit-eater. It is a large prey animal for jaguars in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Lowland paca
nodes.desc: A forest rodent that eats fallen fruit such as figs, and is itself prey for jaguars.

nodes.name: White-lipped peccary
nodes.desc: Roams the forest in herds, rooting for fruit and seeds. Jaguars are recorded preying on it.

nodes.name: Scarlet macaw
nodes.desc: A fruit and seed-eating parrot. Macaws gather at riverbank clay licks in the western Amazon, which is a big draw for visitors to Manú.

nodes.name: Andean cock-of-the-rock
nodes.desc: A cloud-forest bird of ravines and streams. It eats mostly fruit plus insects, and its leks attract predators such as jaguars and ocelots.

nodes.name: Spectacled bear
nodes.desc: South America's only bear, mostly vegetarian: bromeliads, palm nuts, fallen fruit and a little meat. Cloud forest is its best habitat.

nodes.name: Characin fishes
nodes.desc: Piranha and relatives, the main food of giant otters in Amazon rivers and oxbow lakes.

nodes.name: Giant otter
nodes.desc: Family groups hunt fish, mainly characins, in shallow water. Black caimans have been reported preying on them.

nodes.name: Black caiman
nodes.desc: A large lowland river and oxbow-lake predator that eats fish and has been reported taking giant otters in Peru.

nodes.name: Andean condor
nodes.desc: A scavenging bird of the high Andes that glides over the park's highland zone and feeds on carrion.

nodes.name: Jaguar
nodes.desc: The top predator of the lowland forest, eating prey from fish and caiman to peccary and tapir.

nodes.name: Puma
nodes.desc: A big cat found from lowland to montane forest. It can prey on spectacled bear cubs.

nodes.name: Harpy eagle
nodes.desc: A huge forest-canopy eagle that hunts monkeys and sloths. It is listed among the lowland birds of Manú.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Drives growth from the warm lowlands to the cloud-forest slopes.

nodes.name: Rain and cloud mist
nodes.desc: Heavy rainfall and cloud on the Andean slope feed the park's forests and bromeliads.

nodes.name: Meandering rivers
nodes.desc: Rivers and oxbow lakes carry fish and keep shifting the floodplain forest.

nodes.name: Clay licks
nodes.desc: Exposed riverbank clay where parrots and some mammals come to eat soil. Reasons are still debated.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and insects such as dung beetles break down dead leaves, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
